course_description:
This is an issues-based course where students apply their developing sociology skills to real world problems and injustices such as gender discrimination, racism, and income inequality, in Australia and globally. The course content will be dynamic, using current debates and issues as the basis for learning. The assessment will be tailored to address the interests of students. Learning will take place in a blended learning environment with a mixture of online material, and in-class workshop engagement. During classes, the course utilises a collaborative environment that invites students to apply their sociological imaginations to think about how power, social structure, and identity work to create and to resist social inequalities.

Online Modules (Weeks 1-12)

Every week (Weeks 1-12), there is an online module in Blackboard that you must complete before your class. These modules include readings and resources to help you prepare.

In-Person Classes

Most weeks also include an in-person class. These classes are based on the online module content, so you must complete the online module first. If you have not completed the online module, the class discussions and activities may not make sense to you. Please check your timetable and the study guide to confirm which weeks have in-person classes.

course_aims: In this issues-based course, students will apply their developing sociology skills to real world problems of inequality, such as gender discrimination, racism, and rising income inequality, to explore the possibilities for change. Completion of this course will allow students to progress to second year where we expect they will be able to approach more applied methods and sub-discipline based electives with more confidence and better outcomes.

learning_outcomes.description: demonstrate an ability to think sociologically about inequality, including what social inequality is, why it occurs, what its impact is, and possible responses
critically reflect on your own experiences and positionality in relation to inequality and privilege
develop a sense of agency and engage with solution focused social science
develop communication skills to advocate for social justice initiatives

Drawing on concepts learned in the course, and your own research, you will identify a compelling argument for addressing systemic disparities and injustices in a particular area, propose a path of action and present your pitch in a concise and persuasive manner. Please see Blackboard for details of the task, including the scenario, submission requirements, and uploading instructions, as well as the marking criteria that will be used to assess your work. AI Use: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which AI may provide limited support and guidance. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy. Students may be required to complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . learning_activities.topic: Introduction: Welcome & What is Social Inequality? Welcome to week 1 of SOCY1070 which serves as an introduction to the course. There is an online Learning Module for Week 1 to help you get oriented to the course and to provide you with links to some helpful resources and support. You are expected to come to class having read the Course Profile and the Course Study Guide as well as this Learning Module. Building on what you have learned from the Study Guide for the course, in this week’s Tutorial we look at how learning will happen in the course, what you need to do to pass the course, and the resources that will assist you. You will be invited to reflect on your personal connections to the topic of inequality through a critical incident timeline. We will then introduce two key theories that underpin this course.

How do we know if/where social inequality exists? Measurement is one means by which we can recognise the existence of inequality, and understand whether it is changing – for better or worse. However, this is not a neutral, straightforward process: In this week’s Learning Module , we examine the measurement of inequality, via a series of video lectures. Please read the online module prior to your tutorial. Our in-class Tutorial experience provides opportunities to ground these concepts and clarify your understanding.

Why does social inequality matter? (Online only) Welcome to Week 3 of SOCY1070 where we look more closely at why social inequality matters, and why, as social scientists we might be interested in it. Our online Learning Module introduces this topic with interviews, videos and readings. To complement this and assist you particularly with Assessment 2, we also have a Learning Module from the library which helps you with search tips and an orientation to research. As there is a public holiday in Brisbane, there are no face-to-face Tutorials in this course this week, only the online modules for you to complete. Please reach out to your tutors should you need clarity about any of the module material.

What causes social inequality? Our focus this week is on the causes of social inequality. Through the online Learning Module , we begin with the idea of othering, and essentialising the other. We also distinguish between social categorisation and social devaluation and look at how judgement cycles are formed at the individual and social levels and explore the important topic of “unconscious bias”. Please read the online module prior to your tutorial. This week our assessment commences. The Tutorial time will be used to complete the first in our series of in-class exams. You can see further details about Assessment 1 in the course Study Guide. On Blackboard there are additional resources to help you prepare for this task and know what to expect.

Is social inequality inevitable? In this week’s online L earning Module we ask, “Is social inequality inevitable?” by thinking about the history of inequality and how it has manifested over time. We will also ask the question, “So, are things getting better or worse?” and consider whether we are getting closer to equality for all. You might be surprised at the answer. This week we mainly rely on videos for our content so you might want to prepare the popcorn! Please engage with the online module prior to your tutorial. This week’s Tutorial helps pull together the ideas from the last few weeks: why social devaluation matters, why it occurs, and whether it is inevitable.

Inequality and the impact of colonisation Last week we took a broad historical lens to the idea of social inequality. This week we narrow our focus to the specific topic of colonialisation and the impact of colonisation on First nations people. We do this by engaging with the excellent online module “History lives in us”. The online Learning Module examines how events and policies in the past have shaped the identities and experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples today. The module looks at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander activism; the ‘rights’ movement and campaigns waged by key organisations in the lead up to the establishment of the Commonwealth Department of Aboriginal Affairs in 1972. Please read the online module prior to your tutorial. This week’s Tutorial invites further engagement with the module and examines in what ways this history is still powerfully with us and the consequences for first nations people globally and in Australia.

Theories of inequality - Intersectionality and Privilege Often, sociology courses and texts on inequality provide a weekly run-down on different axes of inequality: gender in Week 1, race in Week 2, class in Week 3, and so on. In this course, we have deliberately chosen not to do that, but to instead foreground intersectional understandings of inequality. This week's Learning Module focuses on this idea by introducing the topics of positionality, privilege, intersectionality and compound disadvantage. Please read the online module prior to your tutorial. We will continue this discussion in our Tutorial where we will invite you to think about your own connections to privilege and intersectionality with a series of in-class exercises. As self-identified black, lesbian, feminist, mother, poet, warrior, and cancer-survivor, Audre Lorde (1984) says, “There is no such thing as a single-issue struggle because we do not live single-issue lives.”

Social inequality over time Week 8 focuses on the evolution of inequality over time, examining individual fluctuations and life course perspectives. In Week 8's online Learning Module, Associate Professor Paco Perales's recorded lecture poses the question: does being born poor mean staying poor? We will also delve into intergenerational transmission of advantage/disadvantage, exploring broader societal impacts. Transitioning from micro to macro analysis, we will scrutinise the role of social institutions in shaping equal or unequal societies. Please read the online module prior to your tutorial. In Week 8's Tutorial you will undertake the second of your in-class exams. This task is worth 20% of your grade. You can see further details about the assessment in the course Study Guide.

Theories of inequality - Power/Knowledge For those of you who have previously studied sociology, you were likely introduced to some of key thinkers in sociological theory: Marx, Weber, Durkheim, for example.In the course we continue to reference these important thinkers, but we also want to bring in a different theoretical perspective by thinking about the work of Michel Foucault. This week's Learning Module introduces Foucault's ideas of power/knowledge and discipline, showing how these have shaped our thinking in new and exciting ways and given us new understandings of the dynamics of inequality. Please read the online module prior to your tutorial. In this week’s Tutorial we will apply Foucault’s thinking about power/knowledge and use a jigsaw exercise to help us work through some of his key ideas.

Responding to social Inequality – Solution focused social science (Online only) So far we have spent the semester exploring social inequality – what it is, why it exists, how it can be measured, and its various often devastating impacts. For the last few weeks of semester we are looking at how we might respond, which links to the idea of “Solution focused social science”. Our online Learning Module this week introduces this idea, suggesting that the role of social science is not simply to study phenomena, but to provide solutions towards resolving modern social challenges. As Monday of this week is a public holiday in Brisbane there are no Tutorials scheduled. However, we will be monitoring online communications should you have any queries about the online materials.

What strategies can we use for social transformation? Throughout this course we have highlighted the central concepts of agency and structure. We have spent the last section of the course looking at how structure operates. In this week's online Learning Module we flip to thinking about agency – first of all, how we exercise individual agency, as well as the limits of our individual agency. Then we begin thinking about collective agency, how we can work deliberately to create change in social structures. Please engage with the online module prior to your tutorial. In our Tutorial we will undertake the third of our in-class exams during class-time .

How do I plan for future impact? Join us for our final Learning Module , where we focus on employability and help you use what you have learned in this course, in your thinking about future career options. In our final Tutorial for the semester we work through the ideas of collective agency for change, and provide opportunity for any final conversations about Assessment 2.

Assessment 2 There is no Learning Module or Tutorial during week 13. You are encouraged to use this time prepare your final assessment item for the course (Assessment 2 - due Friday 2pm this week). Your tutors will be available for consultation. They will advise you of the arrangements for this.
